question.text: A pension-fund LP asks Mr. Vikram Singh (Manager, Narmada Mid-Cap AIF) to discuss his 'hurdle rate' and target returns. The PPM states a 15% hurdle. Per Ch 12 guidance on hurdle rate setting in the Indian context, the Manager should defend 15% as:

answer.text: Too low — industry best practice in India is 25% hurdle.
Too high — SEBI caps hurdle at 10% for Category II AIFs.
Arbitrary — hurdle rates have no effect on Manager incentives since they only affect tax.
Reasonable and in context — Ch 12 cites 15% as reasonable; too low (8-10%) makes the Manager's task too easy and yields higher carry, too high (25%) may tempt undue risk-taking.

explanation.text: The Logic: Ch 12 explicitly: 'hurdle rate should be fixed reasonably and in context (say 15% in the Indian context)'. It explains that 8-10% is too low (Manager gets easy carry) and 25% is too high (risk-taking temptation). The Trap: A inverts the chapter. B fabricates a SEBI cap. C is plainly wrong — hurdle drives waterfall economics. Cross-Exam Context: Hurdle/IRR concepts recur in XIX-A/B (for distributor client conversations) but here the Manager must own the justification. In XXI-B (PM), performance-fee hurdles are also nudged by SEBI (high-water mark rules). Manager's Pro-Tip: In LP negotiations, offer a compound (IRR) hurdle rather than simple, and a catch-up after hurdle (80/20 up to a limit). This keeps alignment and protects carry economics.
